fderoles.plain: Several jobs at software companies involve both technical skill and talking to customers. A Sales Engineer helps win the sale, a Solutions Architect designs how the product fits, a Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE) builds and ships the working system at the customer, a Customer Success Engineer keeps a live customer healthy, and a consultant sells hours of expert work. They differ in what they produce, when in the customer's life they work and how much production code they write. An FDE spends most of the week, around 70 to 80 percent, on code and model work.
fderoles.analogy: Think of building a house. The sales engineer is the show-home guide, the architect draws the plans, the FDE is the builder who actually puts up the walls on your plot and fixes what the plans missed, and the customer success engineer is the maintenance contact after you move in. A consultant is the independent inspector you hire by the hour.
fderoles.why: Interviewers often ask how an FDE differs from an SA or a CSE, and a clear answer shows you understand the job. On a real engagement you will receive work from pre-sales and hand it to customer success, so you need to know what each role owns. Knowing the differences also stops you from applying to a job with the wrong title, or skipping the right job because its title is unfamiliar.

subtopics.title: Five roles that work with customers
subtopics.body:
Software companies that sell to large businesses have several technical roles that talk to customers. Their names sound alike, so beginners mix them up. The quickest way to tell them apart is to ask two questions: what does this person produce, and when in the customer's life do they do it?

A Sales Engineer (SE), also called a solutions engineer or pre-sales engineer, works before the sale. They run demos, answer technical questions and sometimes build a small proof of concept so the buyer believes the product fits. A Solutions Architect (SA) designs how the product fits the customer's systems: which data flows where, which cloud services, which security controls. Some SAs work pre-sale, some post-sale, and some are hands-on builders.

A Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE) builds and ships the real, working deployment inside the customer's environment, owns it through go-live, and tells the product team what customers need. A Customer Success Engineer (CSE) looks after a customer who is already live: configuration, troubleshooting, health checks and helping teams use more of the product. They usually work next to a Customer Success Manager (CSM), a non-technical role that owns the relationship and the renewal. A technology consultant, often from an outside firm, sells hours: reports, process design or custom code, delivered under a contract, and the work does not feed back into a product.

The Genesis topic tells the history of the FDE role; this topic compares the roles in detail so you can explain the difference in an interview in one minute.
subtopics.example: A mid-sized insurer, Hollins Mutual (made up), buys an AI claims-triage product. The SE demoed it on sample claims in March. The SA drew the data-flow diagram for the insurer's security team. The FDE spent May and June connecting it to the claims system and tuning it on 20 claim types. Since August, a CSE has run monthly health checks, and an outside consultant wrote the insurer's new claims-handling procedure.

subtopics.title: Where each role sits in the lifecycle
subtopics.body:
A customer lifecycle is the path a company takes from first hearing about a product to renewing the contract. The usual stages are: lead (someone shows interest), evaluation (demos and questions), proof of value (a small test on the customer's own data that proves the benefit), contract, implementation (building and connecting the product), go-live (real users start), adoption (use grows) and renewal or expansion (the customer pays again, often for more).

Each stage has a lead role. The Account Executive (AE), the salesperson, owns the deal; the SE supports them in evaluation; an SA may design the solution; the FDE usually takes over at implementation, sometimes already at proof of value; the CSE and CSM take over after go-live.

The weak points are the handoffs, the moments when work passes from one role to the next. Details get lost: a promise made in a demo, a security concern raised in week one, the name of the one person who really understands the data. A handoff note is a short written summary the outgoing role gives the incoming role. The FDE is on both sides of it: receiving from pre-sales, and handing over to customer success.

Edge case: in small companies one person may do three of these roles. The stages still exist, so the handoff note is still useful, even if you are writing it to your future self.
subtopics.example: At Hollins Mutual, the SE told the claims director in a demo that the product 'reads handwritten notes'. It was not in the handoff. In week three the FDE found that 18 percent of claims had handwritten adjuster notes and the pilot scope did not cover them. One line in a handoff note would have saved a tense meeting and a week of rework.
checklist: What was promised, in the customer's own words
Success criteria and how they will be measured
The demo, its data and any shortcuts it used
Systems to connect and who owns each one
Key people: sponsor, product owner, IT, security
Open risks and objections raised during the sale
Things the customer was told we will not do
Dates already committed

subtopics.title: The time split: 70 to 80 percent code
subtopics.body:
The course material describes FDEs spending around 70 to 80 percent of their time on code and model work. The exact number varies by company and by the phase of a project, but the idea matters: an FDE is an engineer first. That is what separates the role from sales and success roles, where hands-on building is a small part of the week.

What counts as code and model work? Writing integration code against the customer's systems, building data pipelines, writing and testing prompts, running evaluations, tuning retrieval, debugging inside the customer's network, code review and tests. What is the rest? Discovery interviews, demos, status meetings, writing updates and documents, travel and admin.

The split drifts. Customers like talking to the engineer, and every meeting feels important. Two habits protect the build time. First, measure it: log your week for two weeks and look at the numbers. Second, move work to the right person: the engagement manager or Echo (see the Pod operating model topic) owns scheduling and status, and a short written update can replace a 30-minute status call.

Edge cases: in week one of an engagement, discovery may take half your time, and that is correct. In the week before go-live, almost all of it is building and testing. Look at the average over a month, not one day.
subtopics.example: An FDE at a logistics customer logs a 45-hour week. 32 hours are pipeline code, prompt and eval work, debugging and code review: 71 percent. The biggest non-build item is 5 hours of customer meetings. She replaces the Tuesday status call with a written end-of-day note on the shared channel and gets 1 hour back each week.
subtopics.code:
# One week of an FDE's calendar, in hours, grouped by activity
week = {
    "build: pipeline and integration code": 14,
    "build: prompts, evals and model tuning": 9,
    "build: debugging in the customer environment": 6,
    "build: code review and tests": 3,
    "customer meetings and discovery": 5,
    "internal syncs and planning": 3,
    "writing: updates, docs, tickets": 3,
    "travel and admin": 2,
}

total = sum(week.values())
build = sum(h for k, h in week.items() if k.startswith("build"))
share = build / total * 100

print(f"Total hours: {total}")
print(f"Code and model work: {build} h = {share:.0f}%")
for k, h in sorted(week.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1]):
    print(f"  {k:<46}{h:>3} h")
if share < 70:
    print("Below the 70% target: look for meetings to cut or delegate")
# Total hours: 45
# Code and model work: 32 h = 71%
#   build: pipeline and integration code           14 h
#   build: prompts, evals and model tuning          9 h
#   build: debugging in the customer environment    6 h
#   customer meetings and discovery                 5 h
#   build: code review and tests                    3 h
#   internal syncs and planning                     3 h
#   writing: updates, docs, tickets                 3 h
#   travel and admin                                2 h

subtopics.title: A week in the life of an FDE
subtopics.body:
A typical FDE week mixes deep build time with short, focused customer contact. There is no single standard week, but the rhythm below is common for a pilot in its build phase.

Monday starts with planning: look at what the customer's users hit last week, pick the week's goal with the product owner and write it down. Tuesday and Wednesday are build days, often on site, sitting near the users so you can watch them try the new version. Thursday is for evaluation and hardening: run the test set, look at failures, fix the worst ones. Friday is for writing and feedback: a weekly update to the sponsor, notes to your own product team about what customers keep asking for, and cleanup.

Some parts appear every day. A short stand-up with your pod (15 minutes). An end-of-day note in the shared channel. A check of logs and alerts if something is live. A few messages from users, answered quickly or turned into tickets.

On-site versus remote: many FDEs travel to the customer one or two weeks a month, especially early on and around go-live. On-site days go to discovery, shadowing users and demos; remote days go to deep build work. The Life on site topic covers travel rhythm and pace in more depth.
subtopics.example: Week 5 of a claims-triage pilot at Hollins Mutual: the goal is 'route motor claims under $5,000 with 90 percent agreement with senior adjusters'. By Thursday the eval shows 86 percent; the FDE finds most misses are claims with two vehicles, adds a rule, and Friday's update reports 91 percent with the change.

rows: Pod stand-up, pick weekly goal with product owner
Watch 3 adjusters use the new version
Fix what they hit, ship to test

subtopics.title: How titles differ by company type
subtopics.body:
The same title means different jobs at different companies, and different titles can mean the same job. Three company types are worth knowing.

At AI labs and model providers, customer-facing engineers help large customers build with the models: prompts, retrieval, agents, evaluations. Titles you will see include forward deployed engineer, applied AI engineer and solutions architect. Some of these roles are pre-sales and some are deeply hands-on, so read the details.

At data and analytics platforms, similar work is often called professional services, resident solutions architect, or delivery engineer. The engineer may be placed with one large customer for months, building pipelines and models on the platform.

At SaaS companies, look for implementation engineer, onboarding engineer, integration engineer or technical account manager (TAM). A TAM is usually a named technical contact for a big account, focused on support, planning and escalations more than new builds.

Consultancies and systems integrators use titles such as technology consultant or delivery lead. The work can be close to an FDE's, but it is billed by the hour and does not shape a product.

The rule: judge the job by its verbs. 'Build, ship, deploy, own in production' points to FDE-like work. 'Present, advise, support the sales cycle' points to pre-sales. 'Drive adoption, run business reviews' points to customer success.
subtopics.example: Two postings are both titled 'Solutions Architect'. Posting A says 'partner with account teams to run technical discovery and demos'. Posting B says 'build and deploy production integrations in customer environments, write Python daily'. Posting B is an FDE job with a different title; Posting A is closer to a Sales Engineer.
checklist: Which verbs describe the work: build and ship, or present and advise?
What share of the week is hands-on code?
Before the sale, after it, or both?
Is the target measured on deals, adoption or live usage?
How much travel, and on site with one customer or many?
Who owns the code after go-live?
Does feedback reach a product team?

subtopics.title: Moving between these roles in a career
subtopics.body:
People move between these roles often, because they share one core: technical skill used in front of customers. Knowing the common moves helps you plan your own route and explain it in interviews.

From software engineer to FDE: you already build. The gap is customer skills: discovery, handling ambiguity, writing for executives. Prove it with a project where you worked directly with users. From sales engineer to FDE: you already handle customers and demos. The gap is production engineering: tests, deployment, monitoring and owning code after go-live. Prove it with a portfolio project that runs in production-like conditions. From consultant to FDE: you know delivery and client management; the gap is usually depth in one product and in modern AI engineering.

From FDE, common next steps are senior or lead FDE, engineering manager of an FDE team, solutions architect, product manager (FDEs see many customers' needs, which is exactly what product managers need), or founding a company, because FDEs learn a market's real problems.

Edge case: moving from FDE to a pure sales role can feel like a step away from building, and moving from FDE to core product engineering can feel slower, because you lose daily customer contact. Neither is wrong; know what you enjoy.

The Resume and job search topic shows how to write bullets that make any of these moves credible.
subtopics.example: Mei worked three years as a sales engineer at a CRM vendor. To move into an FDE role she built a small invoice-extraction service with tests, a Dockerfile and a monitoring dashboard, ran it for a friend's bookkeeping business for two months, and wrote up the results. In interviews she led with the running system, not the demos.

rows: A project with real users and a written update
An API and pipeline with tests

glossary: Sales Engineer (SE)
A technical person who helps win a sale with demos, answers and small proofs; also called solutions engineer or pre-sales engineer.
Solutions Architect (SA)
A technical person who designs how a product fits a customer's systems; some are pre-sale advisors, some are hands-on builders.
Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE)
An engineer who builds and ships a working deployment inside the customer's environment and feeds what they learn back to the product.
Customer Success Engineer (CSE)
A technical person who keeps live customers healthy and growing through configuration, troubleshooting and health checks.
Customer Success Manager (CSM)
A non-technical role that owns the relationship with a live customer and the renewal.
Account Executive (AE)
The salesperson who owns a deal and the commercial relationship.
Technical Account Manager (TAM)
A named technical contact for a large account, focused on support, planning and escalations.
Professional services
Paid expert work, such as implementation or training, sold alongside a product.
Proof of value
A small test on the customer's own data that shows the product's benefit before or just after the contract.
Handoff note
A short written summary one role gives the next so promises, risks and contacts are not lost.
Customer lifecycle
The stages a customer goes through: lead, evaluation, proof of value, contract, implementation, go-live, adoption, renewal.
practice: Write a one-minute spoken answer to 'How is an FDE different from a Solutions Architect and a Customer Success Engineer?' Record yourself and check that you name what each one produces and when.

Find three job postings with different titles (for example forward deployed engineer, solutions architect, implementation engineer). Highlight the verbs and classify each as pre-sales, build or post-sales.
Log one week of your own work or study time in the categories from the time-split code. Run the script and write two changes that would raise your build share.
Write a handoff note from a sales engineer to an FDE for an invented deal, using every item in the handoff checklist.
Stretch: sketch your own career route from your current role to FDE, using the 'Moving between roles' table, and list the one proof project that closes your biggest gap.

fdeskills.plain: The FDE skill set is the mix of abilities that make someone good at building AI and software systems inside a customer's business. It is often drawn as a radar with five axes: technical depth (building and debugging), problem finding (discovering what is really needed), customer empathy (understanding people), product judgment (deciding what is worth building) and ownership (driving the outcome to the end). A self-assessment is a structured way of scoring yourself on those axes. Done honestly, with evidence, it tells you exactly what to study next.
fdeskills.analogy: It is like a decathlon athlete's score sheet. You do not win by being world-class at one event and failing the rest; you need a decent score in every event and a couple of strong ones. Before training, a coach times you in each event, and the slowest important event is where the next month of practice goes.
fdeskills.why: Interviewers for FDE roles test all five axes, usually in separate rounds, and a candidate who is strong only on code often fails the customer rounds. On the job, the gap shows fast: a brilliant builder who does not find the real problem ships the wrong thing. Knowing your shape early lets you spend your study time where it moves your chances most.

subtopics.title: The five axes of the FDE radar
subtopics.body:
A skills radar is a chart with one spoke per skill. You mark a score on each spoke and join the dots, so the shape shows strengths and gaps at a glance. For FDE work, five axes are commonly used.

Technical depth is your ability to build and debug real software: code, data, APIs, deployment and AI systems. Problem finding (also called problem identification) is the ability to discover what the customer actually needs, which is often different from what they first ask for. Customer empathy is understanding how users and buyers think and feel, listening well and explaining things in their terms. Product judgment is deciding what to build, what to skip and what should become a reusable product feature instead of a one-off. Ownership is treating the customer's outcome as yours: following through, raising problems early and finishing.

Why these five? An FDE sits between a customer and a product. Technical depth lets you build. Problem finding and empathy make sure you build the right thing for real people. Product judgment keeps the build from becoming custom sprawl, which the Moats topic explains. Ownership makes the result actually go live.

Edge case: different companies weight the axes differently. An AI lab may push hardest on technical depth; a SaaS company with long sales cycles may weight empathy and product judgment more. Read the job description and interview guide to see which axes they stress.
subtopics.example: Two candidates apply to an FDE role at a document-AI vendor. Ravi scores 5 on technical depth and 2 on everything else. Lena scores 3 or 4 on all five. Most FDE hiring panels would prefer Lena, because every customer engagement uses all five, and a 2 on empathy or ownership shows up in the first week on site.

rows: Follows tutorials, needs help to debug
Ships and debugs a service end to end
Finds the real blocker behind the ask
Restates the user's view before answering
Spots risks early and closes loops

subtopics.title: T-shaped: one spike plus breadth
subtopics.body:
A T-shaped person has broad, working knowledge across many areas (the top bar of the T) and deep expertise in one (the vertical stroke). FDEs need this shape because a customer engagement touches everything: data extraction, an API, a model, a deployment, a dashboard, a security review. You cannot hand each piece to a specialist on site.

Breadth means you can do the basic version yourself and know when to call for help. For example: write a SQL query and a small API, call an LLM with tools, put a service in a container, read a log. Depth, your spike, is the area where you are the person others ask. Common FDE spikes are data engineering, backend systems, retrieval and evaluation of LLM systems, or infrastructure and security.

How to choose a spike: pick something you already enjoy, that customers pay for, and that you can show. Do not choose the most fashionable area if you have no evidence in it.

How to build breadth: use a checklist of basics and make sure each is at least a level 2. The atlas projects p1 to p9 are designed to cover the breadth: a CSV cleaner, SQL analytics, a FastAPI service, ingestion, Docker, an agent, an MCP server and RAG with evaluations.

Edge case: some people are 'comb-shaped', with two or three spikes. That is fine later in a career. Early on, one clear spike makes you easier to describe and to hire.
subtopics.example: Tomasz is a data engineer moving into FDE work. His spike is pipelines and SQL, level 4. His breadth checklist shows gaps in LLM tool calling and deployment. He spends four weeks on the tools and deploy topics and finishes projects p5 and p6. His resume now reads as 'data engineer who ships AI features', a clear T.
checklist: Write and debug a SQL query with joins and grouping
Build a small REST API with input validation
Call an LLM API, including tool use, and handle errors
Put a service in a container and run it somewhere other than your laptop
Read logs and trace one request end to end
Explain a security review question such as where data is stored
Build a simple evaluation set for an AI feature
Name your spike in one sentence and show one project that proves it

subtopics.title: Ownership and bias to action
subtopics.body:
Ownership means you treat the result as yours, not only your task. In practice it shows as a few habits: you finish things, including the boring parts like docs and tests; you raise problems early with a suggested fix; you follow a problem across team boundaries until someone who can fix it has it; and you close loops by telling people what happened.

Bias to action means that when you are unsure, you take a small, safe step that produces information, instead of waiting for perfect clarity. Build a rough prototype, run a test on 50 records, send a draft. The key word is safe. Separate reversible decisions (easy to undo, such as trying a prompt change in a test environment) from irreversible ones (hard to undo, such as deleting customer data or changing a production schema). Move fast on the first kind and slow down, write it down and get approval on the second.

Ownership is not doing everything yourself. Sometimes the owning move is to hand a task to the right person and check it got done. It is also not hiding bad news until you have fixed it: owners report early.

Edge case: on a customer site, you do not own the customer's systems. Ownership there means making sure the right customer person knows, with evidence, and offering help, not fixing their system without permission.
subtopics.example: At a hospital supplier, an FDE sees that the customer's nightly product export has been arriving two hours late for a week, which delays her AI reorder suggestions. It is not her system. She checks the timestamps, writes a three-line note to the export's owner with the impact (buyers see yesterday's data until 10 a.m.), suggests moving the job earlier and adds an alert on her side. The owner moves the job the next day.
checklist: Did I finish the unglamorous parts: tests, docs, handoff?
Did I raise the risk as soon as I saw it, with a proposed fix?
Is the decision reversible? If not, did I get it approved in writing?
Did I follow the problem to someone who can actually fix it?
Did I tell everyone involved how it ended?
Did I avoid changing a customer system without permission?

subtopics.title: Comfort with ambiguity
subtopics.body:
Ambiguity means you do not have all the facts, the goal is fuzzy or people disagree about what they want. FDE work starts ambiguous almost every time: 'use AI to speed up claims' is a wish, not a spec. Comfort with ambiguity is being able to make steady progress anyway, without freezing and without pretending to be certain.

A simple method has four steps. First, write down what you know and what you are assuming, in two separate lists. Second, pick the assumption that would change the plan most if it were wrong. Third, test it in the cheapest way you can: ask one person, shadow one user for an hour, run a query, build a throwaway prototype. Fourth, decide and write down the decision and what would make you change it. Then repeat with the next assumption.

State your confidence out loud. 'I am fairly sure, about 70 percent, that most delay is in the approval step; I will know by Thursday' is more useful than a vague 'probably'. It tells people how much to rely on it.

Edge cases: ambiguity about goals is harder than ambiguity about facts. If two executives want different things, research will not fix it; you need them to decide, so write a one-page summary of the options and ask for a decision by a date. The Case interview and Discovery topics teach the questioning in depth.
subtopics.example: A regional bank says 'we want an AI assistant for our branch staff'. The FDE lists assumptions: staff mostly ask about products; answers exist in the policy wiki; staff will use a chat window. She tests the riskiest one first by reading 300 real questions from the helpdesk log. 40 percent are about account-opening rules, and only half of those are answered in the wiki. The plan changes to fixing the source documents before building the assistant.

subtopics.title: Rating yourself honestly with evidence
subtopics.body:
Self-ratings are easy to get wrong in both directions. People new to a field often rate themselves too high, because they do not yet know what they are missing. Experienced people sometimes rate themselves too low. The fix is the same for both: rate against evidence and against a fixed scale.

An anchored scale gives each number a plain meaning, so a 3 means the same thing every time you rate. A simple one: 1, I have read about it; 2, I have done it in a tutorial or course; 3, I have done it on a real project with some help; 4, I have done it on a real project alone and could explain every choice; 5, I could teach it and have handled the hard cases.

Evidence is anything you can point to: a repository, a deployed demo, a written story in STAR form (Situation, Task, Action, Result, from the Interview topic), feedback from a manager or customer. A useful rule is to cap your score when evidence is missing: no evidence caps you at 2, one piece caps you at 3. The code below applies that rule.

Then get an outside view. Ask a peer or mentor to rate you on the same scale, and discuss any axis where you differ by two points or more.

Edge case: for people skills, evidence can be a situation rather than an artifact, such as 'calmed an angry user and kept the project on track'. Write it down as a short story so it counts.
subtopics.example: Aisha rates herself 3 on problem finding. When she lists evidence, she has none: in every project she built what the ticket said. The rule caps her at 2. She decides her next project will start with three user interviews and a written problem statement, which becomes her first piece of evidence.
subtopics.code:
# Self-ratings from 1 (never done it) to 5 (could teach it)
ratings = {"Technical depth": 4, "Problem finding": 3, "Customer empathy": 4,
           "Product judgment": 3, "Ownership": 4}
# Pieces of evidence you can point to for each axis:
# a shipped project, a written story, feedback from someone else
evidence = {"Technical depth": 3, "Problem finding": 0, "Customer empathy": 1,
            "Product judgment": 0, "Ownership": 2}

def honest(score, proofs):
    # Rule: no evidence caps you at 2; one piece caps you at 3
    cap = 2 if proofs == 0 else 3 if proofs == 1 else 5
    return min(score, cap)

for axis, score in ratings.items():
    h = honest(score, evidence[axis])
    flag = "  <- claimed more than you can show" if h < score else ""
    print(f"{axis:<17} said {score}, evidence {evidence[axis]}, honest {h}{flag}")
# Technical depth   said 4, evidence 3, honest 4
# Problem finding   said 3, evidence 0, honest 2  <- claimed more than you can show
# Customer empathy  said 4, evidence 1, honest 3  <- claimed more than you can show
# Product judgment  said 3, evidence 0, honest 2  <- claimed more than you can show
# Ownership         said 4, evidence 2, honest 4

subtopics.title: Turning gaps into an atlas route
subtopics.body:
A gap is only useful if it becomes a plan. Turn your honest ratings into a short route: a list of topics, one or two per week, each ending with a concrete output that becomes new evidence.

Step 1: set a target. For a junior FDE role, a 3 on every axis plus a 4 on your spike is a reasonable goal. Step 2: list the axes below target and sort them by size of gap, then by how much the jobs you want care about them. Step 3: map each axis to atlas topics. Step 4: give each topic a week and an output. Step 5: re-rate after about six weeks and pick again.

The mapping below is a starting point. Technical depth grows through the Module 0 to 3 topics and the projects. Problem finding grows through Discovery, the Case method and Debugging. Customer empathy grows through Discovery, Executive communication and Change management. Product judgment grows through Moats, ROI and Proof of concept. Ownership grows through Observability, Last-mile onboarding and Life on site.

Write the route into the learning-plan template so it has dates, outputs and a review point. The Learning routes topic (fluency) shows how to add outside courses.

Edge case: if every axis is below target, start with technical depth to level 2 across the board. Without basic building skills, the people axes have nothing to attach to.
subtopics.example: After honest rating, Aisha has problem finding and product judgment at 2 and the rest at 3 or 4. Her six-week route: Discovery, Case method, Debugging, then Moats, ROI and Proof of concept. Each week ends with an output, such as a written interview guide or a one-page ROI estimate for her own project. In week seven she re-rates and both axes reach 3.

rows: A runbook and a handoff note

subtopics.code:
honest = {"Technical depth": 4, "Problem finding": 2, "Customer empathy": 3,
          "Product judgment": 2, "Ownership": 4}
target = 3  # a solid junior FDE shows at least 3 on every axis
# Atlas topics that build each axis (a starting route, not the only one)
topics = {
    "Technical depth": ["sql", "fastapi", "rag", "evals"],
    "Problem finding": ["discovery", "case", "debugging"],
    "Customer empathy": ["discovery", "exec", "change"],
    "Product judgment": ["moat", "roi", "poc"],
    "Ownership": ["observability", "lastmile", "fieldlife"],
}
gaps = [(target - s, a) for a, s in honest.items() if s < target]
week = 1
for gap, axis in sorted(gaps, key=lambda g: (-g[0], g[1])):  # biggest gap first
    for t in topics[axis]:
        print(f"Week {week}: {t:<10} (builds {axis}, gap {gap})")
        week += 1
print(f"Re-rate yourself after week {week - 1}")
# Week 1: discovery  (builds Problem finding, gap 1)
# Week 2: case       (builds Problem finding, gap 1)
# Week 3: debugging  (builds Problem finding, gap 1)
# Week 4: moat       (builds Product judgment, gap 1)
# Week 5: roi        (builds Product judgment, gap 1)
# Week 6: poc        (builds Product judgment, gap 1)
# Re-rate yourself after week 6

glossary: Skills radar
A chart with one spoke per skill; the shape of the joined scores shows strengths and gaps.
Technical depth
The ability to build, deploy and debug real software and AI systems.
Problem finding
Discovering the customer's real need or blocker, which often differs from the first request.
Customer empathy
Understanding how users and buyers think and feel, and communicating in their terms.
Product judgment
Deciding what to build, what to skip and what should become a reusable product feature.
Ownership
Treating the outcome as yours: finishing, raising risks early and closing loops.
T-shaped
Broad working knowledge across many areas plus deep expertise in one.
Spike
The one area where you are deep enough that others come to you.
Bias to action
Taking a small, safe step that produces information instead of waiting for certainty.
Reversible decision
A decision that is cheap to undo, so it can be made quickly; its opposite needs care and approval.
Anchored scale
A rating scale where each number has a written meaning, so scores stay consistent.
Evidence
Something you can point to that proves a skill: a project, a written story, feedback.
practice: Rate yourself 1 to 5 on the five axes using the anchored scale in this lesson. For each score, write the evidence next to it, then apply the cap rule.
Ask one peer or mentor to rate you on the same scale without seeing your scores. Write down every axis where you differ by two or more points and what evidence explains the difference.
Write one short STAR story for ownership and one for comfort with ambiguity, each under 150 words, with a measurable result.
Run the route script with your own honest scores and turn its output into a six-week plan in the learning-plan template, with one output per week.
Stretch: name your spike in one sentence, then list the breadth checklist items below level 2 and pick the atlas project that closes the most of them.

asyncwriting.plain: Async communication means communication that does not need everyone present at the same time: chat messages, email, shared channels, notes, tickets and pull requests that people read when they can. FDEs rely on it because customers, colleagues and time zones rarely line up. Good async writing puts the important point first, makes any request clear with an owner and a deadline, uses the right channel, and leaves a record others can find later. It also means knowing what should never be written in chat at all.
asyncwriting.analogy: It is like leaving a note for a house-sitter. A good note starts with what matters most ('feed the cat at 7, food is in the top cupboard'), says who to call if something goes wrong and by when, and does not leave the spare key taped to the note. A rambling note with the key attached causes both confusion and risk.
asyncwriting.why: On a customer engagement you might have three meetings a week with the customer but send fifty messages. If those messages bury the ask, the customer's team waits or does the wrong thing, and a day is lost each time. Written updates also replace status meetings, which protects your build time, and a clear written record settles later arguments about what was agreed.

subtopics.title: Bottom line up front
subtopics.body:
Bottom line up front, usually shortened to BLUF, means the first sentence of a message says the most important thing: the answer, the decision or the request. Background comes after. The idea comes from military writing and is now common in business. It works because busy people read the first line in a notification and decide from that whether to open the rest.

A useful shape for any message that needs action has three parts. First, the BLUF line: what you need, from whom, by when, and why it matters. Second, two or three lines of context. Third, links or details for anyone who wants them. In email, put the key point in the subject line too, for example 'Decision needed by Thu: vendor file format'.

Three things make an ask easy to act on: one owner (a named person, tagged, not 'someone' or 'the team'), one deadline (a day and, across time zones, a time), and one question that can be answered quickly, ideally yes or no or a choice between options.

Edge case: some cultures and some executives find a very direct first line abrupt. Keep the BLUF but add one polite word or greeting. Directness is about order, not about being curt. The Executive communication topic covers the pyramid principle for longer documents; this subtopic is about everyday messages.

The code below is a rough checker that flags a long first sentence and a missing ask, owner or deadline. It is a heuristic, not a grammar tool, but it catches the most common problems.
subtopics.example: An FDE at a logistics customer needs a vendor file converted to UTF-8 (a text encoding). Her first draft opens with 'Hi all, so we have been looking at the invoice pipeline this week...' and the ask is in the last line. Her rewrite opens with '@grace we need the vendor file in UTF-8 by Thursday 12:00 to keep the June 8 pilot date.' Grace replies within an hour.
subtopics.code:
import re

def check(msg):
    first = re.split(r"(?<=[.?!])\s", msg.strip(), maxsplit=1)[0]
    issues = []
    if len(first.split()) > 25:
        issues.append("first sentence is long: put the point first")
    if not re.search(r"\?|\bplease\b|\bcan you\b|\bneed\b", msg, re.I):
        issues.append("no clear ask")
    if not re.search(r"@\w+", msg):
        issues.append("no owner tagged")
    if not re.search(r"\b(today|tomorrow|by \w+|monday|tuesday|wednesday|"
                     r"thursday|friday|\d{1,2}:\d{2})\b", msg, re.I):
        issues.append("no deadline")
    return issues or ["looks good"]

before = ("Hi all, so we have been looking at the invoice pipeline this week "
          "and there were a few things that came up around the vendor file, "
          "which might affect the timeline a bit.")
after = ("@grace we need the vendor file in UTF-8 by Thursday 12:00 to keep "
         "the June 8 pilot date. Can you ask the export team? Details below.")
for name, m in [("before", before), ("after", after)]:
    print(name, "->", "; ".join(check(m)))
# before -> first sentence is long: put the point first; no clear ask; no owner tagged; no deadline
# after -> looks good

subtopics.title: Shared channels with a customer
subtopics.body:
A shared channel is a chat channel that people from two companies can both use. Slack calls this Slack Connect; Microsoft Teams has shared channels that can include people from another organisation. Many FDE engagements run day to day in one of these, alongside email for formal items.

Shared channels are fast, but they need rules, because everyone sees everything and messages are kept. Agree the norms in week one and pin them at the top of the channel. Good norms cover: what the channel is for; who is in it from each side; expected response times (for example, within four working hours); using threads so each topic stays together; where decisions are recorded; and what never goes in the channel.

Keep an internal channel as well, for your own team's discussion. Before posting in the shared channel, check you are in the right one; posting internal notes into a customer channel by mistake is a common and painful error.

Write for the whole audience. A developer, the customer's project manager and occasionally an executive may all read the same thread. Explain acronyms the first time, and link to documents instead of pasting long text.

Edge cases: if the customer's security policy does not allow shared channels, use email plus a shared tracker. If a thread turns into an argument, move it to a call, then post a short written summary of what was agreed.
subtopics.example: An insurer and its AI vendor open a channel called #ext-claims-pilot. The pinned note says: purpose, members, 'reply within 4 working hours', 'one thread per topic', 'decisions go in the decision log and are linked here', and 'no customer policy numbers or personal data in this channel'. In the first month, 60 threads are opened and every decision is findable from one link.

rows: Replies stay together and are easy to find
Someone is clearly responsible for answering
Response time agreed, e.g. 4 working hours
People know when to chase and when to wait
Chat scrolls away; the log stays
The channel is visible and kept for a long time

subtopics.title: End-of-day notes and time-zone handoffs
subtopics.body:
An end-of-day note (EOD note) is a short written summary posted when you stop work: what you did, what is next, what is blocked, and what you need from whom. It takes five minutes and saves many messages.

It matters most across time zones. If your customer or a colleague works while you sleep, a good EOD note is a handoff: the next person can start work immediately instead of waiting a whole day to ask you a question. Some teams go further and run a follow-the-sun model, where work passes between regions so it continues around the clock.

A good EOD note has five short parts: Done (with links), Next (tomorrow's plan), Blocked (what stops you and why), Needs (a named person, a question and a time), and Heads-up (anything the reader should know, such as a planned deployment). Keep it to what the reader needs; it is not a diary.

Work out the overlap. The code below converts two teams' working hours to UTC (Coordinated Universal Time, the reference time zone) and shows there is no live overlap between Toronto and Singapore, so the written note is the only handoff.

Edge cases: daylight saving time changes shift the overlap by an hour twice a year, and not every country changes on the same date. If a question cannot wait for the other side's morning, say so clearly and agree an emergency contact route in advance.
subtopics.example: A Toronto FDE and a Singapore colleague share a build. At 17:00 Toronto time she posts: 'Done: retry logic merged (PR 214). Next: load test. Blocked: staging DB password expired. Needs: @arun please rotate it in the vault by your 11:00. Heads-up: deploy to staging at my 9:00.' Arun rotates it in his morning; she starts the load test on arrival.
subtopics.code:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

def work_utc(city_tz, day):
    # 9:00 to 17:00 local time, converted to UTC
    tz, utc = ZoneInfo(city_tz), ZoneInfo("UTC")
    start = day.replace(hour=9, tzinfo=tz).astimezone(utc)
    return start, start + timedelta(hours=8)

day = datetime(2026, 9, 29)
tor = work_utc("America/Toronto", day)
sgp_next = work_utc("Asia/Singapore", day + timedelta(days=1))
print(f"Toronto   {tor[0]:%a %H:%M} to {tor[1]:%a %H:%M} UTC")
print(f"Singapore {sgp_next[0]:%a %H:%M} to {sgp_next[1]:%a %H:%M} UTC")
overlap = min(tor[1], sgp_next[1]) - max(tor[0], sgp_next[0])
print("Live overlap:", max(overlap, timedelta(0)))
print("Singapore starts", sgp_next[0] - tor[1], "after Toronto stops")
# Toronto   Tue 13:00 to Tue 21:00 UTC
# Singapore Wed 01:00 to Wed 09:00 UTC
# Live overlap: 0:00:00
# Singapore starts 4:00:00 after Toronto stops

subtopics.title: Tickets and PR descriptions for their engineers
subtopics.body:
On site you will often write tickets for the customer's teams and pull requests (PRs) that their engineers review. A ticket is a tracked request in a system such as Jira or ServiceNow. A PR is a proposed code change, with a description, that reviewers approve before it is merged. The Git topic covers the mechanics; this subtopic is about the writing.

A good ticket lets a stranger act without asking you anything. It has a specific title ('Vendor export writes Latin-1, breaks UTF-8 parser', not 'File broken'); what happens now and what should happen; exact steps to reproduce; the impact in numbers; the environment; and attachments such as a sample file or log lines, with secrets and personal data removed.

A good PR description answers four questions: what changed, why, how it was tested and what could go wrong (including how to roll it back). Link the ticket. Keep the PR small; a reviewer can check 200 lines carefully but will skim 2,000.

The customer's engineers may have their own rules: a template, a required reviewer, a change-approval board, a style guide. Follow them exactly. Your PRs are a large part of how their team judges you.

Edge cases: if their team is overloaded, a ticket may sit for weeks. Then add the business impact and the date it matters, and raise it with the product owner instead of pinging the engineer repeatedly.
subtopics.example: An FDE's PR at a retailer adds a retry to the price-feed importer. The description states the change in one line, links the ticket, explains that the feed failed 3 times in 2 weeks with a timeout, lists the test (a fake server that fails twice then succeeds), and notes the risk (up to 90 extra seconds on a bad day) and rollback (revert, no data change). It is approved the same day.
subtopics.code:
## What
Retry the price-feed download up to 3 times with backoff (2s, 4s, 8s).

## Why
The nightly import failed 3 times in 2 weeks on a network timeout
(ticket OPS-482). Each failure left store prices one day old.

## How it was tested
- Unit test: fake server fails twice, then succeeds -> import completes
- Unit test: fake server always fails -> job exits with error and alerts
- Ran against staging feed: 1 run, 41,200 rows, no change in output

## Risk and rollback
- Worst case adds about 14 s of waiting before the job fails
- No schema or data changes; roll back by reverting this PR

## Reviewer notes
Only importer/download.py and its tests changed (84 lines).

subtopics.title: Saying no and delivering bad news
subtopics.body:
Sooner or later you must tell a customer something they do not want to hear: a date will slip, a feature will not work, a request is out of scope. Doing it well in writing protects trust.

For bad news, use this order. News first, in one sentence, with the numbers. Then the cause in one or two plain sentences, without blaming individuals. Then the impact on them. Then what you are doing about it. Then any options they can choose between, and the date of your next update. Send it as soon as you know. Bad news that arrives early is a problem to solve; bad news that arrives on the due date feels like a betrayal.

For saying no, avoid a bare refusal. Say what you can do instead, and explain the trade: 'We can add the French documents if we move the delivery receipts to phase two; the end date stays the same.' This turns no into a choice. The Executive communication topic covers negotiating scope with trades in more depth.

When the news is serious, call first, then write. The written message confirms what was said and becomes the record. Never let someone important learn bad news from a channel message they happen to scroll past.

Edge case: if the cause is on the customer's side, state the facts neutrally: 'the export arrived 2 hours late on 4 of the last 5 days' is fair; 'your team keeps breaking the export' is not.
subtopics.example: An FDE learns on Tuesday that accuracy on scanned invoices is 91 percent against a 95 percent target, which puts Friday's go-live at risk. She calls the sponsor at noon, then posts: 'Go-live moves from Fri 12 Jun to Wed 17 Jun. Scanned invoices read at 91% (target 95%). Options: A) go live Friday for text PDFs only, scans follow Wednesday; B) move everything to Wednesday. Please choose by Thu 10:00. Next update Thu 16:00.' The sponsor picks A.
checklist: The news is in the first sentence, with numbers
The cause is stated plainly, without blaming a person
The impact on the customer is spelled out
What we are doing about it is concrete
Options are offered where there is a real choice
There is a decision deadline and a next update time
Serious news was said on a call before it was written
A 'no' comes with what we can do instead

subtopics.title: Tone, brevity and what never goes in chat
subtopics.body:
Tone is how a message feels to the reader. In writing, people cannot hear your voice or see your face, so neutral messages often read as colder than you meant, and jokes or sarcasm are easily misread. Aim for calm, polite and specific. Thank people for concrete things. When you disagree, disagree with the idea and give a reason.

Brevity means removing words that do not help the reader. Cut long warm-ups ('I just wanted to quickly reach out to see if maybe...'), stacked hedges ('it might possibly be that...') and repeated context. Keep the words that carry meaning: numbers, names, dates and links. Short is not the same as vague; 'fixed' is short, 'fixed the date parser, all 2,000 test invoices pass' is short and useful.

Some things should never go in chat, and especially not in a shared channel: passwords, API keys and other secrets; customer personal data such as names with account numbers or health details; internal pricing, discounts and contract talk; opinions about the customer's staff; and guesses about who caused an incident. Chat messages are stored, searchable, may be exported for legal reasons and can be forwarded. Treat every message as permanent.

If you post a secret by mistake, deleting the message is not enough. Tell the owner and rotate the secret, meaning replace it with a new one, straight away. The Security topic explains secrets handling.
subtopics.example: An FDE pastes a database connection string into a customer channel to help debug. It includes the password. She deletes the message within a minute, but the channel had already sent notifications. She tells the customer's IT lead, who rotates the password within 30 minutes and checks the access log, which shows no unknown logins. She adds 'never paste connection strings' to the pinned channel norms.

rows: Share through the approved secrets vault
Refer to a record ID or use a secure file share
Leave to the account executive, by email
Keep feedback factual, raise it privately
Guesses about who caused an incident
State known facts; blame waits for the review

glossary: Async communication
Communication people read and reply to when they can, without meeting at the same time.
BLUF
Bottom line up front: the first sentence states the point or the request.
Shared channel
A chat channel used by people from two organisations, such as Slack Connect or a Teams shared channel.
Thread
A reply chain under one message that keeps a topic together.
EOD note
An end-of-day summary of done, next, blocked and needs, often used as a handoff.
Follow-the-sun
A way of working where tasks pass between teams in different time zones so work continues around the clock.
UTC
Coordinated Universal Time, the reference time zone used to compare other time zones.
Ticket
A tracked request or bug report in a system such as Jira or ServiceNow.
Pull request (PR)
A proposed code change with a description that reviewers approve before it is merged.
Rotate a secret
Replace a password or key with a new one so the old one stops working.
Decision log
A document that records decisions, who made them and why, so they are not lost in chat.
practice: Take the last three work or study messages you sent that asked for something. Rewrite each with a BLUF first line, one owner and one deadline, then run them through the checker code.
Write the pinned 'channel norms' message for a new shared channel with an invented customer, covering purpose, members, response time, threads, decisions and what never to post.
Write three end-of-day notes for three imagined days of a project, using Done, Next, Blocked, Needs and Heads-up. Ask someone to read one and tell you what they would do next.
Write a PR description for a change you made in any project, answering what, why, how tested, and risk and rollback.
Stretch: write the bad-news message for a two-week slip on an invented project, with two options and a decision deadline, then write the call notes you would use before sending it.

ethics.plain: Professional ethics are the standards of honest, fair and careful behaviour expected of someone doing a job for others. For an FDE working at a customer, they cover six areas: keeping the customer's information confidential, handling their data only in approved ways, being honest about what AI can do, avoiding conflicts of interest such as gifts or mixing competitors' information, treating the people whose work is automated with respect, and speaking up when something is wrong. Most of this is written down in contracts and codes of conduct, but on site you apply it through small daily choices.
ethics.analogy: Think of a locksmith or a house cleaner you let into your home. You hand them keys and they see your mail, your valuables and your family. You hire them again only if they never talk about what they saw, never take anything, tell you honestly what the job needs and do not use your house for their own purposes. An FDE is let into a company in the same way.
ethics.why: FDEs get unusual access: production systems, sensitive data, executive meetings and unreleased plans. A single breach of trust, such as customer data pasted into the wrong tool or an inflated accuracy figure, can end an account, create legal liability and follow your career. Customers also watch how you behave when nobody is checking, and those small choices decide whether they trust your code.

subtopics.title: Confidentiality on and off site
subtopics.body:
Confidentiality means keeping private information private. As an FDE you will learn a lot about customers: their systems, security gaps, plans, problems, finances and people. Most of it is covered by a non-disclosure agreement (NDA), a contract saying what information is confidential, how it may be used and for how long. A mutual NDA protects both sides; a one-way NDA protects one. Your employment contract usually adds its own confidentiality duty on top.

Confidentiality is wider than documents. It covers what you see on screens and whiteboards, what you overhear in the office, and what the customer tells you over lunch. A good default: treat everything you learn at a customer as confidential unless you are told it is public.

Practical habits matter more than the legal wording. Lock your screen every time you stand up. Use a privacy filter on your laptop screen when travelling. Do not take customer calls in trains, airports or cafes where others can hear; if you must, use no names. Do not name customers in social media posts, talks or your resume unless your company has written permission to use their name, often called logo rights. Talk about 'a large insurer' instead.

Edge case: information you knew before, or that is genuinely public, is usually not confidential. But if you are unsure whether something is public, treat it as confidential and ask.
subtopics.example: An FDE travelling home on a train opens her laptop to finish a slide about a retailer's store-closure plan. The passenger beside her can see the screen. She closes the file and works on code instead. The next week, a friend asks at dinner which retailer she is working with; she answers 'a large retailer in the north' and changes the subject.
checklist: I know which NDA covers this customer and what it says about duration
My screen locks automatically and I lock it when I stand up
I use a privacy filter when working in public
I take customer calls only where I cannot be overheard
I never name a customer publicly without written logo rights
I describe past customers generically in interviews and on my resume
I ask before treating anything as public

subtopics.title: Customer data on your laptop and in AI tools
subtopics.body:
Customer data is the most sensitive thing you handle. Three rules cover most situations.

First, use only approved tools. A tool is approved when your company and the customer have agreed it may process that data, usually under a data processing agreement (DPA), a contract that says how a vendor may handle personal data. Consumer AI chat apps and personal accounts are not approved, even if they are convenient, because their terms may allow the provider to keep or train on what you paste. Your company's enterprise AI environment may be approved, but check it is covered for this customer's data.

Second, take the minimum. Data minimisation means using only the data you need for the task. For most prompt and pipeline work, a small masked sample is enough. Masking replaces sensitive values such as emails or card numbers with placeholders. The code below shows a first-pass masker. Notice it misses the person's name: regular expressions only catch patterns, so always check by eye, or use synthetic data, which is realistic fake data.

Third, keep it safe and delete it. Store customer data only where the customer allows, on an encrypted disk, never in personal cloud storage. Record where copies live, and delete them at the end of the engagement.

The Compliance topic covers GDPR, HIPAA and data classification in depth, and the Security topic covers secrets and access.
subtopics.example: An FDE wants to test a new extraction prompt on 20 insurance claims. Instead of copying claims into a consumer chatbot, she pulls 20 records into the customer-approved workspace, runs the masker, checks the output by eye and replaces two names the masker missed. She runs the prompt through her company's enterprise API, which the customer's DPA covers, and deletes the sample file that evening.
subtopics.code:
import re

# Order matters: mask long card-like numbers before shorter phone patterns
PATTERNS = [
    ("EMAIL", r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+"),
    ("CARD", r"\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,16}\b"),
    ("PHONE", r"\+?\d[\d ()-]{7,}\d"),
    ("POLICY", r"\bPOL-\d{6}\b"),  # this customer's policy number format
]

def mask(text):
    counts = {}
    for label, pattern in PATTERNS:
        text, n = re.subn(pattern, f"[{label}]", text)
        counts[label] = n
    return text, counts

row = ("Claim from Jane Doe, jane.doe@example.com, policy POL-204417, "
       "call +61 2 5550 1234, refund to card 4111 1111 1111 1111.")
clean, counts = mask(row)
print(clean)
print(counts)
# Regex masking is a first pass, not a guarantee: the name is still there
print("Name still visible:", "Jane Doe" in clean)
# Claim from Jane Doe, [EMAIL], policy [POLICY], call [PHONE], refund to card [CARD].
# {'EMAIL': 1, 'CARD': 1, 'PHONE': 1, 'POLICY': 1}
# Name still visible: True

subtopics.title: Honesty about what the model can do
subtopics.body:
Customers often expect AI to be either magic or useless. Part of your job is to give them an accurate picture, even when a rosier one would make the next meeting easier.

Overpromising takes several forms. Stating accuracy without conditions ('it is 97 percent accurate') when that number came from clean, typed documents and the customer has many scans. Showing a demo on hand-picked examples and letting people assume it is typical. Saying 'it will learn from corrections' when nothing in the system actually retrains. Promising a date before you have seen the data.

Honest statements have three parts: the number, the conditions under which it was measured and the known weak spots. For example: '97 percent field accuracy on 500 typed invoices from the last three months; scans are lower, around 90 percent, and handwritten notes are not supported yet.' Measure on a held-out test set, meaning data the system was not tuned on, or the number will be too high. The Evals topic explains how.

'I do not know yet, and I will find out by Thursday' is an honest and professional answer. So is 'this is not a good use of AI; a rule would work better'.

Edge case: salespeople or your own managers may push for a more optimistic message. You can support a positive message while keeping the facts accurate; if you are asked to state something false, raise it, as the last subtopic explains.
subtopics.example: Before a steering meeting, an account executive asks the FDE to say the claims model 'handles all claim types'. It handles 14 of 20 types well. The FDE suggests: 'handles the 14 most common claim types, which are 88 percent of volume, at 93 percent agreement with senior adjusters; the other 6 are planned for phase two.' The sponsor later says this clarity is why she approved phase two.

rows: 97% on 500 typed invoices; scans are around 90%
Corrections are logged; we retrain monthly after review
It handles the 14 types that are 88% of volume
We will be live in 4 weeks
4 weeks if the data export arrives by the 10th
The AI will not make mistakes
It will make some; here is how people catch them

subtopics.title: Gifts, conflicts and competitors
subtopics.body:
A conflict of interest is a situation where your personal interest could influence, or look like it influences, a decision you make for your employer or the customer. Most companies have a written code of conduct that covers this. Read yours; the details differ between companies.

Gifts and hospitality: customers and partners may offer meals, event tickets or presents. Many companies allow small, occasional gifts and require you to declare anything above a set value, and some customers forbid their own staff from accepting anything. Public-sector customers usually have much stricter rules, and anti-bribery laws such as the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and the UK Bribery Act make offering or accepting anything that looks like an inducement a serious matter. When unsure, decline politely or declare it.

Side work and relationships: doing paid work for the customer on the side, recommending a supplier where a friend or relative benefits, or holding shares in a company you are evaluating are all conflicts. Declare them and step back from the decision.

Competitors: FDEs often work for several customers in the same industry. Information from one customer never goes to another: not data, not documents, not their pricing, not their unreleased plans. You may reuse general skills and your own company's product knowledge. At a customer, you may also see a competitor of your own employer's product; do not dig for their confidential details.

Edge case: 'we built this for another customer' is fine to say about your company's own reusable product feature, but not about custom work or ideas that belong to that other customer.
subtopics.example: An FDE works with two regional banks. Bank A shows her its new fraud-scoring rules. Two months later, Bank B asks 'what are other banks doing about card fraud?'. She answers with general, public patterns and the capabilities of her company's product, and says she cannot share other customers' approaches. At Bank B's year-end, she is offered concert tickets worth several hundred dollars; she checks her company policy, which requires approval above a small limit, and declines.
checklist: I have read my company's code of conduct and gift policy
I declare gifts and hospitality above the policy limit
I apply stricter rules for public-sector customers
I declare side work, investments and relationships that touch my work
I step back from decisions where I have a personal interest
I never move data, documents or ideas between customers
I reuse only general skills and my own company's product knowledge

subtopics.title: Automation and the people affected
subtopics.body:
Much FDE work automates tasks that people do today: reading documents, answering questions, routing requests. That can make jobs better by removing tedious work, and it can also shrink or change roles. Decisions about staffing belong to the customer, but how you behave affects real people.

First, be honest with users. The people you shadow and interview often guess that the system may change their jobs. Do not tell them it will not affect them if you do not know. Ask the sponsor early how the change will be explained to staff, and align with that message. If the sponsor wants the purpose hidden from the people you are interviewing, raise it, because it also damages the project: people who feel misled stop helping.

Second, design for people. Keep humans in charge of decisions where errors cause harm, give users an easy way to correct the system, and make the system's limits visible. The Responsible AI topic covers human oversight and fairness in depth.

Third, respect formal processes. In some countries, employee representatives such as works councils or unions have a legal right to be consulted on new technology that monitors or changes work; in Germany, for example, works councils have co-determination rights over technical systems that can monitor employee performance. Ask the customer's HR or legal team whether this applies before rollout.

Edge case: if a customer asks you to use the system to monitor individual staff performance in ways they have not been told about, treat it as a concern to raise, not a feature request.
subtopics.example: At a freight company, an FDE is automating invoice data entry that takes 12 clerks most of their day. Before shadowing, she asks the sponsor what staff have been told. The sponsor explains the clerks will move to handling carrier disputes, which are backlogged. The FDE repeats that message consistently, involves two senior clerks in testing, and designs a review screen so clerks approve every invoice above $10,000.

subtopics.title: When to raise a concern, and how
subtopics.body:
An ethical concern is anything that seems dishonest, unsafe, unfair or against the law or policy. Common FDE examples: being asked to misreport results, to use data beyond what people agreed to, to hide a known risk from the customer, to ship a system you believe will harm users, or to skip a required security or privacy review.

Raise it early. Small concerns are easy to fix in week two and very hard in week ten. Use a ladder, moving up only when the step below does not resolve it. Step 1: check the facts and your understanding; ask a clarifying question, because sometimes there is a good reason you did not know. Step 2: raise it with the person directly and suggest an alternative. Step 3: raise it with your manager, in writing. Step 4: use your company's formal ethics, legal or compliance channel. Many companies also have a confidential reporting line, sometimes called a whistleblowing or speak-up line, and many countries give legal protection to people who report certain wrongdoing in good faith.

Write it down. A short, factual note with the date, what happened, why it concerns you and what you suggest keeps the discussion calm and creates a record. Stick to facts, not accusations.

Edge case: if there is an immediate risk of harm to people, such as a safety system behaving dangerously, stop or pause the work first if you are able to, then escalate straight away without climbing the ladder step by step.
subtopics.example: An FDE is asked by a customer manager to include in a training set chat transcripts from customers who were told their data would be used 'only to answer your question'. She asks whether consent covers training (step 1); the manager says 'nobody will know'. She suggests using only transcripts from after a consent update (step 2), then writes to her manager with the facts (step 3). Her company's legal team confirms training is not covered, and the project uses the newer transcripts.
subtopics.code:
CONCERN NOTE  (to: my manager, cc: none)   Date: 14 Oct

What happened
  On 13 Oct the customer's data lead asked us to add 18,000 support
  chat transcripts (Jan to Jun) to the fine-tuning set.

Why it concerns me
  The chat notice at the time said data is used 'only to answer your
  question'. Training may not be covered by that consent.

What I have done
  Asked the data lead (13 Oct); told 'it will be fine'.
  Paused adding the transcripts; nothing has been trained on them.

What I suggest
  Use only transcripts after the 1 Jul consent update (about 9,500),
  and ask our legal team to confirm by 17 Oct.

glossary: Non-disclosure agreement (NDA)
A contract that defines confidential information, how it may be used and for how long.
Logo rights
Written permission to name a customer publicly, for example in marketing or talks.
Data processing agreement (DPA)
A contract that sets how a vendor may handle personal data on a customer's behalf.
Data minimisation
Using only the data needed for a task, and no more.
Masking
Replacing sensitive values with placeholders so a sample can be shared more safely.
Synthetic data
Realistic but fake data made to look like real records, used for testing.
Held-out test set
Data kept aside and never used for tuning, so accuracy measured on it is realistic.
Conflict of interest
A situation where a personal interest could influence, or seem to influence, a work decision.
Code of conduct
A company's written rules for ethical behaviour, including gifts and conflicts.
Works council
An elected body of employees that, in some countries, must be consulted on changes to work.
Whistleblowing line
A confidential channel for reporting suspected wrongdoing.
practice: Find and read your current or a past employer's code of conduct (or a public one from a large company). Write down the gift limit, the declaration process and the reporting channel it describes.
Run the masking code on five invented records you write yourself, including names and addresses. List what the masker missed and add one pattern that catches a missed item.
Rewrite three overpromising sentences about an AI system you know into honest versions with a number, conditions and known weak spots.
Write a one-page concern note for this scenario: a customer asks you to turn off the human review step two days before go-live to hit a date. Use the structure from the last subtopic.
Stretch: write the answer you would give in an interview to 'Tell me about a time you pushed back on something you thought was wrong', using a real or realistic situation in STAR form.
